title: GPT-1: predict the next word, then do the task—where pretrain + fine-tune became standard
summary: GPT-1 first trains a 12-layer Transformer decoder to “predict the next word” on more than 7,000 books, then casts every task as a single text sequence and fine-tunes. One general model sets new records on 9 of 12 datasets. We unpack the pretraining and fine-tuning equations, the input transformations, the ablations, and the early zero-shot signs—then look at how they split into BERT and GPT-2.
ai_summary: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (OpenAI, 2018) first pretrains a 12-layer, 768-dimensional Transformer decoder with a language-model objective on more than 7,000 books, then fine-tunes on labeled data for each task, adding only a linear output layer and packing sentence pairs, questions, and answer choices into one delimiter-separated text sequence. It sets new records on 9 of 12 datasets: Story Cloze improves by 8.9 points, RACE by 5.7, and GLUE reaches 72.8. Removing pretraining drops the average from 74.7 to 59.9; zero-shot experiments without fine-tuning also improve steadily as pretraining progresses, foreshadowing GPT-2.
brief: Problem: labeled data is scarce, unlabeled text is plentiful; pretrained word embeddings only transfer word-level information, and there is no good way to transfer higher-level knowledge.
Method: pretrain a 12-layer Transformer decoder on BooksCorpus with next-word prediction, then pack each task's input into one text sequence and fine-tune with an added linear layer.
Results: new records on 9 of 12 datasets; removing pretraining costs 14.8 points on average, and swapping in an LSTM costs 5.6; zero-shot ability rises steadily with pretraining.
Limitations: unidirectional, every task still needs fine-tuning, and small; BERT went bidirectional, GPT-2 chose to scale up and drop fine-tuning.

paper.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
paper.authors: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever

cover.headline: A close read of the original GPT-1 paper
cover.highlight: Predict the next word first, then do the task

blocks.p: In June 2018, OpenAI's Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, and Ilya Sutskever released this 12-page paper. It did not appear on arXiv—just as a preprint on OpenAI's website—and later became known as **GPT-1**: GPT is the Generative Pre-Training in the title.

The method has two steps. First, **pretraining**: take a 12-layer Transformer decoder and train it to “predict the next word” on more than 7,000 unpublished books, with no human labels. Second, **fine-tuning**: on a small amount of labeled data for each specific task—judging whether two sentences contradict each other, answering reading-comprehension multiple choice, classifying sentiment, and so on—attach a simple output layer and continue training. To make every task fit the same model, the paper **packs structured inputs such as sentence pairs, questions, and answer choices into a single text sequence**, so the model architecture barely changes.

The result: a general model not designed for any particular task set new records on 9 of 12 datasets, improving commonsense reasoning (Story Cloze) by 8.9 points and reading comprehension (RACE) by 5.7. Remove pretraining, and the average score drops by 14.8 points.

This paper established the standard NLP approach for the next few years: **pretrain on massive unlabeled text, then fine-tune on the specific task**. BERT, released four months later, kept the same framework but switched to a bidirectional encoder; GPT-2 and GPT-3 stayed decoder-only and kept scaling, leading to today's large language models.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: GPT-1 = a 12-layer Transformer decoder pretrained on more than 7,000 books with next-word prediction + a linear layer fine-tuned after each task's input is packed into one text sequence. One general model beat purpose-built models on 9 of 12 datasets, showing that what generative pretraining learns can transfer.

callout.title: Three concepts you need before reading
callout.text: Don't worry if they're new; these three are enough:
list: **Transformer decoder**: the half of the Transformer responsible for generation. Each position can see only the words before it (masked self-attention). See our Transformer close read.
**Language model**: predicts the next word from the preceding words. Training one needs no human labels—any text works.
**Fine-tuning**: take a pretrained model and continue training on new-task data for a while, nudging its parameters toward the new objective.

sections.h: Problem: too little labeled data, almost unlimited unlabeled text

blocks.p: Natural language understanding covers many tasks: textual entailment (judging whether one sentence follows from another), question answering, semantic similarity, and text classification. Every task needs human-labeled data, and labeling is slow and expensive. The paper opens by noting that large amounts of unlabeled text are everywhere, but labeled data is scarce, and models trained only on labeled data struggle.

The most successful approach for using unlabeled text at the time was **pretrained word embeddings** (word2vec and its relatives), covered earlier in this series. But those only transfer information at the word level. Transferring higher-level knowledge—sentence structure, semantics, common sense—has two problems:

list: **What objective to pretrain with**: language modeling, machine translation, discourse coherence—each approach won on some tasks and lost on others, with no consensus.
**How to transfer to downstream tasks**: some built task-specific structures on top of the pretrained model, some used intricate learning schemes, some added auxiliary objectives—all awkward.

callout.title: Read widely first, then practice the specific task
callout.text: Have a student read a lot first (pretraining) and they will pick up grammar, common sense, and how stories go without realizing it. Later, a small set of targeted exercises (fine-tuning) gets them up to speed quickly. That is far easier than having a student who has never read anything learn reading comprehension from a few thousand practice questions alone. GPT-1 turns this intuition into a system that set records on 9 tasks.

blocks.p: Similar ideas had been tried before GPT-1: Dai and Le (2015) and Howard and Ruder (ULMFiT, 2018) pretrained LSTM language models and then fine-tuned for text classification. The paper argues that LSTMs can use only a short context range, while Transformers capture longer-range structure. It also sets out to prove the approach works on a wider range of tasks than text classification.

The pretraining objective is the standard language-model objective: given a large unlabeled text U = {u_{1}, …, u_{n}}, maximize the sum of the log probability of each word given the k words before it.

parts.desc: The i-th token in the text.
Context window size: the maximum number of tokens the model can look back. GPT-1 uses 512.
All parameters of the neural network.
The sum of log probabilities for guessing each position correctly. Maximizing this makes the model predict the next word as accurately as possible.

plain.title: A giant game of “what comes next”
plain.text: Pretraining is a giant game of “what comes next”: given the preceding words, guess the next one. The higher the probability of guessing correctly, the better. It can only look backward (green arrows); it cannot peek at what follows. To guess well, the model has to learn grammar, common sense, and how context fits together.

blocks.p: The model is a **decoder-only Transformer**: token embeddings plus position embeddings are the input, which passes through 12 Transformer blocks; finally the transposed token embedding matrix is applied and passed through softmax to produce next-word probabilities.

parts.desc: Token embedding matrix: one row vector per token.
Position embedding matrix: GPT-1 uses learned position embeddings rather than the original Transformer's sinusoidal functions.
A Transformer block: masked multi-head self-attention + position-wise feed-forward network.
The output layer reuses the transposed embedding matrix instead of adding new parameters: input goes word → vector, output goes vector → word, using the same table.

plain.title: Look up, stack 12 layers, look up in reverse
plain.text: First use the vocabulary to turn each word into a vector and add the position vector; then pass it through 12 Transformer decoder layers; finally use the same vocabulary in reverse to compute the probability of each word in the vocabulary being the next word. The same table is used on the way in and the way out.

callout.title: Why decoder-only?
callout.text: The original Transformer has an encoder (reads) and a decoder (writes), designed for translation. A language model only needs to predict the next word from the preceding text, so it uses just the decoder half: each position can see only the words to its left, enforced by a mask so the model cannot peek at the answer. This decoder-only design continued into the GPT series and most large language models today.

blocks.p: **Pretraining data** is BooksCorpus: more than 7,000 unpublished books across adventure, fantasy, romance, and other genres. The paper particularly emphasizes why it chose this dataset: books contain **long stretches of contiguous text**, so the model can learn to use long contexts. The alternative of comparable size—the 1B Word Benchmark used by ELMo—is shuffled at the sentence level, destroying long-range structure. GPT-1 reaches a perplexity as low as 18.4 on this corpus.

blocks.p: The paper does not state the parameter count directly. It can be estimated from the Transformer arithmetic (about 12 × d^{2} parameters per layer):

fig.title: GPT-1: about 117M parameters, roughly a quarter in the vocabulary
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: an estimate by this site based on the paper's configuration; vocabulary size is taken as about 40,000 from BPE's 40,000 merges.
rows: Reuses token embeddings; not counted separately
fig.note: The GPT-2 paper says its smallest model (117M parameters) is “equivalent to the original GPT,” which matches this estimate. For comparison, the previous article's Seq2Seq had 384M parameters, and GPT-3 has 175B.

blocks.p: **Fine-tuning settings**: most tasks reuse the pretraining hyperparameters, with 0.1 dropout added to the classifier, a learning rate of 6.25 × 10^{-5}, and batch size 32. The learning rate warms up for the first 0.2% of steps, then decays linearly. Fine-tuning is fast—**3 epochs is enough for most tasks**.

sections.h: Step 2: fine-tuning, and turning every task into one text sequence

blocks.p: During fine-tuning, a labeled sample—input tokens x_{1}, …, x_{m} and label y—is fed through the pretrained model, the final-layer output at the last position h_{l}^{m} is taken, and a new linear layer W_{y} is added for classification:

parts.desc: The final Transformer layer's output at the last input token. Because the decoder can only look left, the last position has “seen” the entire input.
The only new weight matrix added during fine-tuning (apart from a few delimiter vectors).
The task's own objective: predict the label correctly.
The optimized objective: the task objective plus λ times the language-model objective, with λ = 0.5. It keeps doing next-word prediction on the task data as an auxiliary objective.

formula.note: The paper says adding the auxiliary language-model objective has two benefits: it improves generalization of the supervised model and speeds up convergence. But the ablation later shows this benefit does not always hold.

plain.title: Practice the task, review the basics
plain.text: Fine-tuning mainly trains on the new task (L_{2}), but the paper also adds a little of the original next-word practice (λ · L_{1})—like doing targeted exercises while reviewing fundamentals. The paper finds this helps on tasks with more data; on small datasets, the effect is less clear.

blocks.p: The truly clever part is the **input transformation**. During pretraining the model has only seen continuous text, but many tasks have structured inputs: a pair of sentences, or a passage plus a question plus several answer choices. The older approach was to build a task-specific structure on top of the pretrained model, which introduces many parameters that were never pretrained. GPT-1 instead **concatenates structured inputs into a single sequence** with special delimiter tokens. All transformations add randomly initialized start and end tokens at the beginning and end.

fig.title: Four task types, all packed into one text sequence for the same model
fig.subtitle: Illustration based on Section 3.3 and Figure 1 of the paper; <s> is the start token, $ is the delimiter, <e> is the end token (its output is used for classification).
rows: Linear layer judges entailment, contradiction, or neutral
Sentence A and sentence B (no natural order)
<s> A $ B <e> and <s> B $ A <e>, each computed once
Add the two outputs element-wise, then apply a linear layer
Passage z, question q, candidate answers a_{k}
One sequence per answer: <s> z q $ a_{k} <e>
Score each sequence and softmax over all candidates
fig.note: The two sentences in a similarity task have no natural order, so both orderings are computed and added, making the result insensitive to order.

plain.title: Change the format, keep the same model
plain.text: Classification, inference, and QA used to each require a dedicated model. GPT-1's approach is to rewrite the input as one text sequence: a start token <s>, an end token <e>, and a delimiter $ between two segments. With the format unified, the same pretrained model only needs one final layer added to handle all these tasks.

callout.title: Use format instead of architecture
callout.text: This is a far-reaching idea: instead of changing the model for each task, rewrite the task into a format the model already knows. GPT-1 only went halfway, still training a linear layer per task. By GPT-2 and GPT-3, even that step is gone: write the task as text (“Translate into French: …”) and let the language model continue. Today's prompts are this idea taken to its logical end.

quiz.q: When fine-tuning GPT-1, what new parameters does the model need?
options: A whole set of new Transformer layers
Only the output layer W_{y} and a few vectors for delimiters and start/end tokens
quiz.why: The paper stresses that the only extra parameters during fine-tuning are W_{y} and the delimiter embeddings. That is the payoff of input transformations: structured inputs are packed into text, so there is no need to build task-specific networks. It took GPT-3's few-shot learning to go further and drop W_{y} as well.

sections.h: Results: new records on 9 of 12 datasets

blocks.p: The paper evaluates on four task types across 12 datasets, ranging from about 5,700 examples (STS-B) to about 550,000 (SNLI). Many baselines are models designed specifically for one task, and some are ensembles of multiple models.

fig.title: Natural language inference: leads on four of five datasets, with RTE the exception
fig.subtitle: Accuracy in %, from Table 2 of the paper. “5x” means an ensemble of 5 models. Blue columns are GPT-1.
fig.note: RTE has only 2,490 examples, making it one of the smallest datasets. The paper speculates that multi-task training would help, but it did not try it.

fig.title: Question answering and commonsense reasoning: Story Cloze improves by 8.9, RACE by 5.7
fig.subtitle: Accuracy in %, from Table 3 of the paper. “9x” means an ensemble of 9 models. Amber columns are GPT-1.
fig.note: RACE is a reading comprehension dataset drawn from Chinese middle and high school English exams, with more reasoning-heavy questions than datasets like SQuAD. Story Cloze asks the model to choose the correct story ending from two options.

fig.title: Classification and semantic similarity: CoLA jumps from 35.0 to 45.4, GLUE total 72.8
fig.subtitle: From Table 4 of the paper, all evaluated on the GLUE benchmark. mc is Matthews correlation coefficient, acc is accuracy, pc is Pearson correlation coefficient. Blue columns are GPT-1.
fig.note: SST-2 and MRPC did not beat the previous best. CoLA improved the most, which the paper sees as evidence of the “linguistic intuition” the model learned from pretraining.

blocks.p: Putting the three tables together: 9 of the 12 benchmarks—SNLI, MNLI, QNLI, SciTail, RACE, Story Cloze, STS-B, QQP, and CoLA—set new records; 3 did not: RTE, MRPC, and SST-2. Often, GPT-1 as a single model beat the baselines' multi-model ensembles.

sections.h: Analysis: what did pretraining actually bring?

blocks.p: **Every layer helps.** The paper transfers only the first few layers of the pretrained model to downstream tasks and observes how performance changes. Transferring word embeddings alone already helps; each additional Transformer layer helps more. On MultiNLI, transferring the full model is 9 points better than transferring only the embeddings. This suggests every layer of the pretrained model learned something useful for downstream tasks, not just the word-embedding layer.

fig.title: Ablation: removing pretraining drops the average from 74.7 to 59.9
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 of the paper; unweighted average across several GLUE tasks and RTE. Amber is the full model.
fig.note: The original table also includes MRPC, QQP, and RTE columns, omitted here. The LSTM beats the Transformer on only one dataset, MRPC.

list: **Pretraining is the key**: without pretraining, the average drops by 14.8 points and every task gets worse; STS-B falls from 82.0 to 30.9.
**Transformer beats LSTM**: with the same framework and a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM instead, the average drops by 5.6 points.

**The auxiliary objective is inconsistent**: it helps on large datasets such as natural language inference and QQP, but not on small datasets. The main text says the auxiliary objective improves generalization, but in Table 5 the average **without** it (75.0) is actually slightly higher than the full model (74.7).

blocks.p: **Zero-shot signs.** The most prescient part of this section is the “zero-shot behavior” experiment: with no fine-tuning at all, use only the pretrained language model and some clever “heuristics” to do the tasks:

fig.title: No fine-tuning: the language model alone can do tasks
fig.subtitle: Compiled from Section 5 of the paper
rows: Append “very” after the sentence, then compare the model's next-word probabilities for “positive” and “negative” and choose the higher one
Compute the average log probability of each token in the sentence, then classify it as grammatical if it exceeds a threshold
Condition on the passage and question, then choose the answer with the highest average log probability
Replace the pronoun with each candidate and check which replacement makes the following text more probable

blocks.p: The paper finds that as pretraining progresses, these zero-shot methods improve **steadily and continuously**; LSTM zero-shot performance is more erratic. The authors' conjecture: to predict the next word more accurately, the language model is forced to learn many tasks along the way. This sentence is almost the outline of the GPT-2 paper.

quiz.q: Why does zero-shot SST-2 add “very” after the sentence?
options: To make the next word naturally an adjective, then compare whether “positive” or “negative” is more likely
To trigger the model's classification layer
quiz.why: “This movie was great. very ___” is more naturally continued with “positive” than “negative”. By constructing a prefix, the model turns a classification problem into a “what's the next word” problem and can answer directly with a language model. This is the core idea behind later prompt engineering.

list: **The GLUE gain doesn't add up**: the introduction claims a 5.5-point improvement on GLUE, but in Table 4 the GLUE total is 72.8 vs. 68.9, a difference of only 3.9.

**The auxiliary-objective claim doesn't match the data**: Section 3.2 says the auxiliary language-model objective improves generalization and speeds convergence, but in Table 5 the average without it is slightly higher. Section 5 is more accurate: large datasets benefit, small datasets don't.
**Two numbers for one task**: Table 2 gives MNLI-m as 82.1, while the full model in the Table 5 ablation scores 81.8 on MNLI. The paper does not say whether they use the same evaluation set.
**The “14.8% drop” is actually a point difference**: after removing pretraining, the average falls from 74.7 to 59.9, a drop of 14.8 points, or about 20% in relative terms.
**Unidirectional**: the decoder only reads left to right, so each position cannot see later text. This is a real limitation for understanding tasks such as classification and question answering.
**Still needs per-task fine-tuning**: although the architecture changes are small, each task still requires labeled data and a trained linear layer.
**Small scale**: about 117M parameters and more than 7,000 books. The conclusion suggests the model and long-text data are both keys to its success, but leaves open what happens with further scaling.

blocks.p: **The story after** came quickly:

list: **Four months later, BERT (October 2018)**: Google kept the “pretrain + fine-tune” framework but switched to a bidirectional Transformer encoder, pretrained with a fill-in-the-blank masked language model, and beat GPT-1 by a wide margin on understanding tasks. The BERT paper uses GPT-1 as its main comparison and deliberately sets BERT-BASE to the same size as GPT-1.

**Eight months later, GPT-2 (February 2019)**: OpenAI chose the other path: keep the architecture, scale to 1.5 billion parameters, replace the data with 40 GB of web text, and **skip fine-tuning entirely**, applying the model zero-shot. This is the scaled-up version of the zero-shot experiments in Section 5 of GPT-1, and the next article in this series.
**After that**: GPT-3 used few-shot learning to discard fine-tuning entirely; InstructGPT brought “fine-tuning” back in another form, to align the model with human intent.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: Why did the paper choose BooksCorpus over the similarly sized 1B Word Benchmark for pretraining?
options: Because books contain long contiguous text, while the 1B Word Benchmark is shuffled at the sentence level, destroying long-range structure
Because the 1B Word Benchmark is too large
quiz.why: GPT-1 needs to learn to use long contexts. In sentence-shuffled data, neighboring sentences have no connection, so the model cannot learn cross-sentence structure. This is also the basis for the paper's claim that it can exploit longer-range information than LSTM methods.

quiz.q: For textual entailment, how does GPT-1 feed the premise and hypothesis into the model?
options: Send them into two separate models
Pack them into one sequence: start token, premise, delimiter, hypothesis, end token
Average the word vectors of the premise and the hypothesis
quiz.why: This is the paper's “input transformation”: pack the structured input into one text sequence, separate it with a delimiter, and feed the output at the end token into a linear layer. That avoids designing a task-specific network for entailment.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What do “pretraining” and “fine-tuning” each do? Why doesn't pretraining need labeled data?
Why does GPT-1 use only the Transformer decoder?
Why can the output layer reuse the token embedding matrix?
What is the auxiliary language-model objective? Why is its effect inconsistent?
How are the four task types each packed into one text sequence? Why is the similarity task computed twice?
What are the three takeaways from the ablation experiments?
How are the zero-shot experiments done? What did they foreshadow?
From GPT-1, which two directions did BERT and GPT-2 take?
